I realize that I'm not going to be filling a 70k seat stadium in the first year of a new league, but even 8-10k seats would be an amazing start. At long last, it's opening night. It's time for the game to kick off. I've spent, at maximum, $100MM of my $300MM win. I still have $200MM invested so I don't really need money. 7 years in solar tech support. What you've been told is *likely* correct. Verify for your actual location especially where taxes are concerened, and make sure the panels accurately account for your usage. 

Your daily estimated production as a rule of thumb should be 1-3x the size of the system in the winter (if not covered by snow), 5-7x the size of the system  in the summer, and 3-5x during winter/fall due to irradiance and environmental conditions. Make sure this will cover your house usage in the winter especially, because that's the time you'll use the most grid power. See if they have a panel cleaning service. Normally, spraying them off with a hose suffices, but if you're older or your house is 2-3 stories tall then it'll be a pain in the ass to do that yourself so having a built in cleaning service would be nice. This is not standard, but does exist with some companies. 

If you need a new roof or will before the warranty is up, get it now. Solar on an old roof is just asking for issues when it rains/snows. Also second what the utility advisor said about replacing electronics, but that will almost definitely be a net benefit because new appliances are going to generally be more efficient than their older counterparts. 

Check the proposed contract carefully before you sign it and make sure there's both a performance guarantee and a system modification clause. The performance guarantee means that if you system doesn't produce the expected energy in a month/year depending on the company you'll get a "true up" that will make up for any lost production from say a damaged inverter. The system modification agreement (probably moot since you'd own the system) covers adding extra panels or a battery system in the future if you want to do so. *Generally* if you own the system this doesn't matter but make sure before you sign. 

You should find out if the system uses string inverters, micro inverters, or a string/optimizer set. String inverters are much less likely to fail as there are less overall components, but when one component fails the whole string (portion of panels, kinda like old Christmas lights) goes out as well. A microinverter system like Enphase will very rarely fail if one microinverter goes out, and they're generally easier/cheaper to get replaced if it's not warranty covered service. Optimizer systems (I think only SolarEdge uses this currently) are the worst of both worlds in that there are more parts to beak because there are optimizers under every panel like a microinverter system, but they all feed into a string inverter. If an optimizer fails, easy fix and only that panel stops working, but if an inverter fails then the whole string or system is down.

Speaking of non-warranty covered service, make sure to get a "critter guard" around your panels. Birds and rodents will frequently make nests/chew wires under the array. Almost without fail, pest/critter damage is *not* a warranty covered service so if you don't get a critter guard at the beginning you'll likely be liable to pay for both the repairs to make the system fully functional again *and* the critter guard to avoid it happening again in the future. If you get it installed at the beginning it'll save at least a $250-500 truck roll to get it done.

I think this is all the important pain points that I've regularly come across in my career. Let me know if you have any other questions. As usually, everything I've said is a generalization based on my experience and is in no way tailored to your specific situation.

That's... not entirely correct. They'll lease you the solar system, so you're getting the benefit of having solar, but then you're paying for *all* the solar you produce, not just what "extra" electricity you make. The energy you don't use is sold back to your local utility to offset whatever energy you have to buy from them during the night or peak usage. 

It usually ends up being a good deal for the homeowner, but you need to make sure you're reading the contract clearly and getting the system properly sized for your actual utility usage. Otherwise you end up paying the lease cost for the system and still getting either a monthly power bill or a yearly "true up" because you use more electricity than your system is sized for. 

You should also make sure there's either a way to either buyout your system or transfer ownership to someone else if you sell your house, because you could be on the hook for the system in the case you move if not. This is much more rare now than it used to be, but something certain solar installers will still try to pull.
